content.title: What is Pattern Matching?
content.description: Pattern Matching is the process of finding whether a smaller string (pattern) exists within a larger string (text) and determining its position.

content.content: Whenever you use Ctrl + F in a document, search for a keyword on Google, filter emails, or find a contact in a messaging app, pattern matching algorithms are working behind the scenes.

content.title: Real-World Importance
content.content: Pattern matching powers search engines, plagiarism detectors, DNA sequence analysis, cybersecurity systems, spam filters, and text editors.

content.title: Key Terminology
content.description: Text is the larger string in which searching is performed. Pattern is the smaller string we want to locate.

content.content: The simplest approach is to compare the pattern with every possible position in the text. If all characters match, the pattern is found. Otherwise, shift the pattern by one position and try again.

content.title: Naive Matching Process
steps: If mismatch occurs, shift by one
Stop when match is found or text ends

content.title: Limitation
content.content: Naive matching performs many unnecessary comparisons when the text is large.
Imagine searching a word inside a 500-page book. Rechecking every character repeatedly would be slow. Advanced algorithms reduce unnecessary comparisons and improve performance dramatically.
KMP is one of the most famous pattern matching algorithms. Instead of restarting comparisons from the beginning after a mismatch, it uses previously computed information to skip unnecessary work.

content.title: Key Idea of KMP
content.description: Use an LPS (Longest Prefix Suffix) array to determine how far the pattern can safely shift after a mismatch.

content.title: Interview Favorite
content.content: KMP is one of the most frequently asked pattern matching algorithms in coding interviews.
Rabin-Karp uses hashing to compare strings. Instead of comparing every character, it first compares hash values and performs detailed comparison only when hashes match.

items.question: Search Engines
items.answer: Finding matching keywords in billions of web pages.

content.title: Finding a Name in a Phonebook
content.content: Searching for a friend's name in a phonebook is similar to pattern matching. Instead of checking every page repeatedly, smart strategies help you jump directly to likely locations.

content.title: Interesting Fact
content.content: Google Search processes billions of pattern matching operations every day to return relevant results within milliseconds.

items.question: What is the most common mistake?
items.answer: Confusing substring generation with pattern matching.

items.question: Why do naive solutions become slow?
items.answer: Because they repeatedly compare the same characters.

items.question: When should KMP be used?
items.answer: When searching patterns efficiently in large texts.

content.title: Interview Insight
content.description: If an interviewer asks about efficient string searching, KMP and Rabin-Karp are usually the expected algorithms.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Pattern matching searches a pattern inside a text.
Naive matching compares every possible position.
KMP uses an LPS array to avoid redundant comparisons.
Rabin-Karp uses hashing for faster matching.
Pattern matching powers search engines and text editors.
KMP and Rabin-Karp are important interview topics.
